glossary.bourse.def: A market where financial securities are bought and sold: company shares, government and corporate bonds. Prices change constantly, according to supply and demand.
glossary.bourse.example: Euronext in Paris, the NYSE and the Nasdaq in New York.
glossary.action.def: A slice of ownership in a company. Shareholders can receive part of the profits (the dividend) and vote at general meetings. If the company does well, the share gains value; if not, it loses value.
glossary.action.example: A company split into 1,000 shares: if you own 10, you own 1% of the company.
glossary.obligation.def: A loan made to a government or a company. It pays back on a set date and pays interest in the meantime. Usually less risky than a share, but it often earns less.
glossary.obligation.example: Buying a French government bond means lending money to France.
glossary.indice-boursier.def: A number that tracks a basket of shares: it is a stock market's thermometer. When people say "the market went up", they usually mean its index.
glossary.indice-boursier.example: The CAC 40 tracks 40 large companies listed in Paris; the S&P 500, 500 large US companies.
glossary.etf.def: A fund you buy on the stock market like a share, which copies an index: in a single purchase, you own a small piece of every company in the index. Fees are usually low, but you gain and lose exactly like the index.
glossary.etf.example: An S&P 500 ETF rises when the 500 large US companies rise as a whole, and falls with them.
glossary.dividende.def: The share of profits a company pays out to its shareholders, usually once a year. It is never guaranteed: a struggling company can cut it or scrap it.
glossary.dividende.example: A company paying €2 per share: with 10 shares, you receive €20.
glossary.capitalisation.def: A company's total value on the stock market: the price of one share multiplied by the number of shares. It changes every day with the share price.
glossary.capitalisation.example: 1 billion shares at €50: the company is worth €50 billion on the market.
glossary.risque-rendement.def: They go hand in hand: the more an investment can earn, the more you risk losing. A risk-free investment earns little.
glossary.risque-rendement.example: A guaranteed savings account earns little; a share can earn a lot, or lose half its value.
glossary.diversifier.def: Spreading your money across several investments, companies, countries or sectors, so you don't lose everything if one of them collapses.
glossary.diversifier.example: Don't put all your eggs in one basket: an ETF diversifies across hundreds of companies at once.
glossary.introduction-bourse.def: The moment a company first offers its shares to the public. It raises money to grow, and its founders can sell part of their stake.
glossary.introduction-bourse.example: A young company listing in Paris or New York to fund new factories.
glossary.opa.def: An offer made to all of a company's shareholders to buy their shares at a set price, often above the market price, in order to take control.
glossary.opa.example: When a takeover bid is announced, the target company's share often jumps towards the offered price.
glossary.krach.def: A sudden, steep fall in stock prices, often triggered by panic: everyone wants to sell at the same time.
glossary.krach.example: The Wall Street crash of October 1929, or the fall of stock markets during the 2008 crisis.
glossary.taux-de-change.def: The price of one currency expressed in another. It moves every day with the economy, interest rates and confidence in each country.
glossary.taux-de-change.example: If the euro rises against the dollar, a trip to the United States costs a European less.
glossary.matieres-premieres.def: The price of a resource traded on world markets: oil, gas, copper, wheat, gold… A war, a drought or a discovery can make it soar or plunge.
glossary.matieres-premieres.example: Brent, North Sea oil, is the benchmark price in Europe.
glossary.valeur-refuge.def: An investment that investors turn to in a crisis because it is considered safe.
glossary.valeur-refuge.example: When a war breaks out, gold and the Swiss franc often rise.
glossary.volatilite.def: How much, and how fast, a price moves. A very volatile share can gain or lose a lot in a few days.
glossary.volatilite.example: Shares in young tech companies are often more volatile than those of large groups.
